name: 11th Street Bar
pitch: A proper neighborhood Irish pub that fills to the walls when Liverpool or a World Cup match is on, and the bartenders somehow keep everyone poured. Off match days it is a laid-back room with fair prices and a crowd that talks to strangers.
perfect: a big match needs a loud, friendly room
insider: Sunday nights after 9 bring traditional Irish music and Monday is jazz, no cover, so tip the musicians.

name: 12th St. Ale House
pitch: An old-school belly-up-to-the-bar joint on 2nd Ave with a seasonal beer list, a real jukebox and murals outside and in. Drinks are strong and fairly priced, and the longtime bartenders know the neighborhood better than anyone.
perfect: you want a cheap, unfussy pint with a jukebox
insider: Bring singles for the jukebox and tip in cash; the regulars do, and the bartenders will treat you like one.

name: 2A
pitch: A two-story corner standby at Ave A and 2nd: a dim old-school bar downstairs and a lounge upstairs with big windows over the avenue. Drinks are simple and strong, there is live music some nights, and it goes until 4 a.m. every night.
perfect: you want a window seat over Avenue A after midnight
insider: Head upstairs for the window seats; the sidewalk tables wobble, so hold your drink.

name: 310 Bowery Bar NYC
pitch: A roomy brick-walled bar on the Bowery with Edison bulbs, a lot of TVs and surprisingly good pizza. Sundays are mellow and the bartender will talk you through the list; weekends bring a DJ and the sports crowd.
perfect: your group wants pizza, a game and room to spread out
insider: Go on a Sunday evening for a quiet seat at the bar and an espresso martini with a slice.

name: 7B / Horseshoe
pitch: The corner bar on 7th and B that has been in half the movies shot in the East Village, and it still runs on a punk jukebox and a photobooth. It is a no-nonsense dive, so order simply, tip properly and you will be treated like a regular.
perfect: you want the classic Alphabet City dive, no frills
insider: The jukebox is the best thing in the room; bring singles and take your turn in the photobooth.

name: A10 Kitchen
pitch: Under new owners since late 2025, this Avenue A spot has turned into the kind of place people come back to five times in a summer. Burgers and small plates are solid, but the spritzes and the warm welcome from the owners are the reason to go.
perfect: a long, easy happy hour with a pitcher of spritz
insider: Order the Hugo spritz, and check the bill for an automatic gratuity before adding a tip.

name: Accidental Bar
pitch: A tiny natural-sake bar on Avenue C where the owner pours you tastes until you find the one you like. It is quiet enough to hear yourself think, the small plates are good, and the prices are kinder than you expect.
perfect: you want to learn sake from someone who loves it
insider: Tell Austin what you usually drink and let him pick; it is only open Wednesday through Saturday from 5.

name: Ace Bar
pitch: A big Alphabet City game room of a bar: pool tables, dart boards, pinball, skee-ball, a claw machine and a photobooth. It is built for groups and the happy hour is generous; just know the door can be strict and the crowd gets loud late.
perfect: ten friends need skee-ball and cheap pitchers
insider: Come early on a weeknight to claim a dart board before the groups roll in.

name: Alphabet City Beer Co.
pitch: Half beer bar, half bottle shop on Avenue C, with a cheese counter and a staff who will talk you into a sour you have never heard of. It opens at 9 in the morning for coffee and laptops, then turns into the neighborhood's easiest hang by evening.
perfect: you want a serious beer list without the attitude
insider: Ask for the cheese plate with the Vermont cheddar, and check the fridge for rare cans that never make the board.

name: Amor y Amargo
pitch: A tiny, candlelit bar on Avenue A built entirely around amaro and bitters: no juice, no shakers, nothing sweet. The bartenders are the friendliest experts in the neighborhood and will steer you to a drink you did not know you wanted.
perfect: you want a serious stirred drink before dinner
insider: It fills by 7 on weekends with nowhere inside to wait, so go on a weeknight or at opening at 5 and order the Spanish olives.

name: Amsterdam Billiard Club
pitch: Twenty-five pool tables plus ping-pong, darts and foosball under one big roof near Union Square, with a full bar and decent food. It is roomy and surprisingly quiet, so you can actually talk between shots.
perfect: a rainy afternoon needs a pool table and a pint
insider: Weekday afternoons are the time for a free table; drinks run high, so eat first or come for happy hour.

name: Artichoke
pitch: The 14th Street counter where the artichoke slice is a meal: thick, creamy, heavy and worth the hype. There are no seats and the line can crawl at peak, but it is open until 5 a.m. every night, which is exactly when you want it.
perfect: it is 3 a.m. and you need one enormous slice
insider: One artichoke slice is dinner for two; if you want a second flavor, make it the crab.

name: Au ZA'ATAR
pitch: Avenue A Lebanese with a reclaimed-wood room, sidewalk tables and a tableside shawarma spit that is the thing to order for a group. The hummus and shish tawook are the reliable picks, and it is open 11 to 11 every day.
perfect: a big group wants to share mezze and shawarma
insider: Get the hummus with mushrooms and pine nuts and the sumac fries, and sit outside on a sunny afternoon.

name: Augurs well Bar
pitch: A brick-walled beer bar at the east end of St. Marks with a deep craft list and a kitchen that punches way above a bar's. The tacos are the surprise, the burger is the deal, and it is open late every night.
perfect: you want good beer and a real dinner for under twenty
insider: Before 7 the unlisted special is a burger, fries and a house lager for about fifteen dollars; ask for it.

name: Avant Garden
pitch: A snug, candlelit vegan spot on 7th Street where the mushrooms do the heavy lifting and nothing on the plate feels like a substitute. It is a splurge, it is romantic, and it is the place to bring a skeptic.
perfect: a date night where no one misses the meat
insider: Share three to five plates between two, start with the artichoke toast, and leave room for the lava cake.

name: B-side
pitch: A woman-owned dive on Avenue B with lounge seats up front, a pool table and foosball in back and a jukebox that goes everywhere. Drinks are strong and cheap, the bartenders are warm, and it hosts the occasional art show or movie night.
perfect: a low-key Thursday with foosball and a strong pour
insider: Claim the couches by the front window early; the back fills up once the pool table gets going.

name: Balvanera
pitch: A candlelit Argentine spot on Stanton where the steak is the point: well-charred outside, tender inside, with empanadas and provoleta to start. Service is attentive even when the room is full, and brunch is the quiet way in.
perfect: you want a proper steak and Malbec without the steakhouse bill
insider: Skip the two-person feast and order the steak and empanadas a la carte; it eats better for the money.

name: Bar Primi
pitch: A two-floor Italian room on the Bowery that does pasta first and does it well: rigatoni alla vodka, light ricotta gnocchi, a whipped-ricotta toast you will want twice. Come early and a booth is easy; come late and it hums.
perfect: pre-show pasta near the Bowery
insider: Start with the whipped ricotta toast with honey and nuts, and get the frozen cocktail in summer.

name: Bar Snack
pitch: A modern neighborhood bar on 2nd Ave run by cocktail veterans, where the frozen drinks are inventive and the snacks lean Irish chip shop. It is buzzy and friendly, and there is usually a seat if you wait a few minutes.
perfect: you want a serious cocktail without a reservation
insider: Order the Split Ends or whatever frozen drink is on, and the spice bag to share.

name: Bar Veloce
pitch: A slim, old-world wine bar on 2nd Ave with a long by-the-glass list and a happy hour that runs 3 to 7 every single day, weekends included. It is a quiet, grown-up stop before dinner rather than a place to settle in for the night.
perfect: a cheap glass of wine before a dinner reservation
insider: Come between 3 and 7, even on Saturday, for seven-dollar glasses; the few sidewalk seats go first.

name: Barcade
pitch: The St. Marks branch of the arcade-bar original: rows of vintage cabinets, a long craft draft list and a crowd that just wants to drink and play. On a good night it is the most fun room on the block; on a packed weekend, less so.
perfect: you want pinball and a draft list, not small talk
insider: Bring cash for the quarter machine, go on a weeknight for free cabinets, and happy hour runs until 8.

name: Beauty Bar
pitch: A 1960s beauty parlor turned bar on 14th Street, dryer chairs and all, where a martini comes with a manicure if you time it right. Early it is kitsch and comedy; after 11 the back room opens and it turns into a dance party.
perfect: you want a manicure with your martini and then dancing
insider: Ask about the drink-and-manicure deal in the early evening, and stay past 11 when the back room DJ starts.

name: Beetle House
pitch: A Tim Burton-themed bar and restaurant on 6th Street where costumed characters wander the room and the cocktails come smoking. It is pricey and theatrical, and if that sounds fun to you, it absolutely is.
perfect: a birthday for someone who keeps Halloween year-round
insider: It is only open Thursday through Sunday; book for dinner but walk in for drinks, and try the mint margarita.

name: Benemon
pitch: A cozy Japanese spot on 4th Street built around rice bowls, with a sake list worth lingering over. The unagi don is the one everyone comes back for; the small plates are where the kitchen shows off.
perfect: a quiet weeknight bowl and a carafe of sake
insider: Get the unagi don and the tuna tataki; weekend lunch from noon is the easiest time for a table.

name: Berlin
pitch: A low-ceilinged basement room on Avenue A with a stage the size of a rug, which means you are standing right in front of the band. Shows are cheap, the sound is better than it should be, and the crowd is there for the music.
perfect: you want to see a punk band from three feet away
insider: Check who is playing before you go; a twenty gets you three bands, and there is no drink menu, so just ask.

name: Beron Beron
pitch: A small, unfussy Japanese place on 1st Ave with a long menu of home-style dishes: omurice, katsu curry, bento boxes, fried oysters. The traditional floor seating is fun and the three-dollar beer is a real thing.
perfect: a cheap, casual Japanese dinner for one or two
insider: Skip the sushi rolls and order the cooked dishes, especially the pork katsu curry, and book the floor-seating table.

name: Bibi Wine Bar
pitch: A small, candlelit wine bar on a quiet stretch of 4th Street with a list that leans natural and a happy hour that is the best wine deal in the neighborhood. Share a bottle and a few snacks and you will leave under eighty dollars.
perfect: a midweek date on a wine-bar budget
insider: Before 8 a full bottle is about thirty dollars and apps are eight; ask for a window seat and order the meatballs.

name: Big Bar
pitch: A tiny red-lit room on 7th Street with vinyl DJs, cheap cans and a bartender who expects you to know what you want. It is cash only and has house rules on the wall, but if you play along it is one of the best low-key hangs around.
perfect: a quiet drink with one friend under red light
insider: Bring cash, order quickly, and go early on a weeknight when there is actually a seat.

name: Blue & Gold
pitch: The old Ukrainian dive on 7th Street: wooden bar, jukebox, pool table, cheap pours and bartenders who do not suffer fools. Bring in takeout from the block, put your name on the pool table and stay a while.
perfect: you want the cheapest honest drink on 7th Street
insider: The pool table always has a wait on weekends, so come on a weeknight and bring your own food.

name: Blue Haven
pitch: A big Irish sports bar on Houston that will put any game you ask for on a screen, with a kitchen that does fried chicken better than the rest of the menu. On Knicks nights tables get reserved, so plan ahead or stand at the bar.
perfect: your crew needs a table for a big game
insider: Order the buttermilk chicken, skip the chili, and reserve a table ahead if it is a game night.

name: Bob white
pitch: A small fried-chicken counter on Avenue C where the tenders are crisp, the mac and cheese is baked and the house sauce does a lot of work. You order at a kiosk and food lands in minutes, so it is lunch, late dinner and takeout all at once.
perfect: you want fried chicken fast and done right
insider: Get the tenders with the house sauce and chimichurri aioli, add the baked mac and a raspberry iced tea.

name: Bobby's Night Out
pitch: A roomy bar and grill on Avenue C with a patio, a wall of TVs and a bottomless brunch that locals swear by. Service can go missing on slow afternoons, so it is at its best when there is a game on and the place is busy.
perfect: a long bottomless brunch on the patio with a game on
insider: Saturday brunch opens at 11:30; grab a patio table and check your card receipt before you leave.

name: Boka
pitch: A basement Korean spot on St. Marks that is really about one thing: crackly fried chicken in garlic-soy or spicy, with fries on the side. The long bench tables swallow big groups and the room runs loud and student-heavy.
perfect: a dozen friends want wings and pitchers
insider: Ten garlic-soy wings feed two; bring cash just in case, and flag your server down rather than waiting.

name: Book Club
pitch: A bookstore on 3rd Street with a real bar, a backyard and board games, open from 9 in the morning until well past midnight. It is the rare place where reading alone with an Aperol spritz is the normal thing to do.
perfect: a solo afternoon with a book and a cocktail
insider: Head for the back courtyard, bring your own book or pick one off the shelf, and go before 6 to get a seat.

name: Bua
pitch: A corner bar at the far end of St. Marks with a big sidewalk patio made for people-watching and a long daytime happy hour. The kitchen does Thai and sushi, the non-alcoholic list is real, and it runs until 4 a.m.
perfect: a sunny afternoon drink with a view of St. Marks
insider: Come in the afternoon for happy-hour cocktails on the patio and order the cheese wontons.

name: Buenos Aires
pitch: A family-run Argentine steakhouse on 6th Street where the staff have been there forever and the owner stops by your table like an uncle. Skirt steak with chimichurri is the move, the Malbec list is deep, and it is open from noon every day.
perfect: you want a serious steak in a neighborhood room
insider: Order the skirt steak medium-rare with extra chimichurri, and ask for the back room if you are more than six.

name: Bull McCabe's
pitch: A low-key Irish dive on St. Marks with a pool table, dart boards and a small patio out back, where the regulars will fold you into their birthday party. Drinks are fairly priced and the bartenders set the tone.
perfect: a casual night of pool with people who talk to you
insider: Weekday evenings after 4 are the time for the pool table; weekends it runs until 4 a.m.

name: Burp Castle
pitch: A monastery-themed beer bar on 7th Street where the bartenders shush you, politely, if you get loud. The Belgian and Trappist list rotates, the oil paintings are absurd, and an hour of whispering over a strong ale is a real reset.
perfect: you need a quiet pint and a mental reset
insider: Go on a weeknight before 8; weekends are packed and the tiny room has maybe twenty seats.

name: Bus Stop Cafe (West Village)
pitch: An old-school West Village diner with booth seating, a sidewalk patio and a menu long enough to feed a picky group. Portions are big, the cocktails are the cheapest around, and it opens at 7:30 every morning.
perfect: a no-fuss breakfast with a big group
insider: Sit on the patio, order the penne vodka or an omelette, and skip the eggs Benedict.

name: Cafe 81
pitch: A small, dim espresso bar on 7th Street with a serious piccolo and a pastry case that is the real draw: olive oil cake, a cinnamon bun, a crisp tomato-and-cheese bread. Seats are few, so most people stand at the counter or carry it to the park.
perfect: you want the best espresso within a block of Tompkins
insider: Order the tomato cheese bread and the olive oil cake, both baked in house, and expect to stand.

name: Cafe Maud
pitch: The 2nd Ave all-day spot that is always full of people who planned their outfit, and it turns out the food backs it up. The smash burger and garlic-dip fries are the order, the frozen Aperol spritz is the drink, and the sidewalk seats are the point.
perfect: a weekend brunch that turns into afternoon spritzes
insider: Skip the line by hitting the coffee window for a maple latte, or come on a weeknight for the burger.

name: Cafecito
pitch: A small Latin coffee shop on Avenue C that does cafe con leche, batidos and a short list of hot empanadas with a mild salsa verde. It is a quick, friendly stop on the way to the L, not a place to camp with a laptop.
perfect: a weekday breakfast empanada on the way to the train
insider: Two empanadas run about nine dollars; get the chicken-and-spinach, and note it is closed Sundays.

name: Caravan of Dreams
pitch: The East Village's longest-running vegan restaurant, on 6th Street, with raw and cooked dishes, organic everything and live jazz on weekend afternoons. It has its off days lately, but a Sunday lunch with a band in the corner is still lovely.
perfect: a lazy Sunday lunch with live jazz and plant-based plates
insider: Go for Sunday lunch when the band plays, order the seitan nachos, and skip the carrot cake.

name: Charlie Bird
pitch: A lively two-level Italian-American room on King Street with a 90s hip-hop soundtrack and a menu that knows its hits: farro salad, Tuscan fried chicken, the pastas. The quick weekday lunch is one of the better deals downtown.
perfect: a business lunch that does not feel like one
insider: Do the two-course quick lunch, start with the complimentary focaccia and the fried chicken, and add oysters.

name: Cherry Tavern
pitch: A dark, unassuming dive on 6th Street with a pool table, a good jukebox and bartenders who make drinks fast and remember you. It is rarely too loud or too packed, which in this neighborhood is a feat.
perfect: a post-show drink and a game of pool
insider: It opens at 6 and is closed Mondays; come before 8 for happy hour and first dibs on the table.

name: ChikaLicious Dessert Bar
pitch: A tiny dessert counter on 10th Street where you sit at the bar and watch a three-course sweet tasting get plated in front of you. Portions are small and the flavors are odd in the best way; it is an experience, not a sugar fix.
perfect: a date needs a dessert course somewhere else
insider: Book ahead for a seat at the counter, order the tasting menu, and add a pot of tea.

name: Chloe 81
pitch: A basement lounge on Ludlow that has quietly been the go-to for downtown birthday parties for years, with a DJ, a long bar and a street-level room added upstairs. Book it right and the staff take care of everything; book it loosely and you may end up sharing the space.
perfect: you need a dance floor for forty friends
insider: Reserve in writing with a headcount and confirm the DJ start time; the basement is the room you want.

name: Claw Daddy's
pitch: A loud, happy seafood-boil joint on Orchard where bags of crab legs and shrimp land in a spicy house sauce and you eat in gloves. Service is quick and warm, and the weekend happy hour oysters and wings are the cheap way in.
perfect: you want to get messy with a seafood boil
insider: Order the boil in the house sauce at medium heat, add rice to soak it up, and know tables turn in about ninety minutes.

name: Clinton Bakery (edge of East Village)
pitch: The Clinton Street pancake institution, where the stack with warm maple butter is as good as everyone says and the Sunday line is as long. Weekday mornings and the Wednesday-to-Saturday dinner service are how locals actually get in.
perfect: someone visiting insists on famous pancakes
insider: Go on a weekday before 10 or book dinner; order the blueberry pancakes and a biscuit, and skip the salad.

name: Club Cumming
pitch: A small, glittery queer bar on 6th Street with a different show most nights: drag, cabaret, karaoke, a themed tea dance. It is inclusive to its bones, the drinks are fairly priced, and even a slow Tuesday feels welcoming.
perfect: you want a dance floor where everyone is welcome
insider: Check the calendar before you go; themed parties and tea dances fill up, while early weeknights are easy.

name: Conor's Goat
pitch: A clean, bright Irish bar on Avenue A that does the neighborhood things well: pub trivia, nachos, a good beer list and a staff that will find room for thirty of your friends. Weekend brunch starts at 11 and runs boozy.
perfect: your group needs a reliable bar with trivia and nachos
insider: Bring a scannable U.S. ID, since the door will not take international cards, and ask which night is trivia.

name: Brick Lane
pitch: A British-style curry house on 2nd Ave where a robot wheels your food to the table and a cup of tomato soup arrives before you have ordered. The spicing is deep rather than strictly traditional, the portions are generous, and the lamb biryani is loaded.
perfect: you miss a proper London curry house
insider: Order the samosa chaat and a paratha to start, and ask about the papadum if you are vegan; it is not.

name: Coopers Craft and Kitchen
pitch: A gastropub on 2nd Ave with a long craft beer and cider list and bar food people actually come back for: truffle fries, grilled cheese with smoked tomato soup, nachos that hold up. The big front windows open onto the street in warm weather and the room works for two or a table of ten.
perfect: a weekday happy hour with real food
insider: Weekday happy hour runs into trivia night, and one weekday has $10 sandwiches, so grab a seat by the open window early.

name: Coyote Ugly Saloon
pitch: The 14th St outpost of the saloon chain, with bartenders dancing on the bar, bras hanging from the ceiling and leopard-print tables, loud and rowdy by design. Go for frozen margaritas and the show, not a quiet drink, and expect a crowd once the evening gets going.
perfect: you want a loud, rowdy bar-top show night
insider: Come late afternoon on a weekday if you want the wings and a bar seat before the crowd and the dancing start.

name: Cozy Cafe
pitch: A hookah lounge on E 1st St where the owner greets you at the door, the couches are deep and nobody rushes you out. It runs until 4 a.m. every night, which makes it the natural landing spot after a comedy show or a game.
perfect: you need a late, unhurried place to land after midnight
insider: You can queue your own music from the table, so bring a playlist, and ask for the Blue Mist if you cannot decide.

name: Crab Du Jour
pitch: A small, casual Cajun seafood boil spot on 1st Ave where the bags of crab legs, shrimp and crawfish come with gloves and a bib. Portions are generous and a combo feeds two, though seasoning has been uneven lately and there is no alcohol, so think messy early dinner rather than night out.
perfect: you want to crack crab legs with your hands
insider: Order the combo for two and ask for extra seasoning on the bag; the kitchen goes light unless you say so.

name: Craft + Carry
pitch: A craft beer bar and bottle shop on St Marks with rotating drafts, cans to go and staff who will steer you to the right IPA or sour without a lecture. There is a backyard, a bowling arcade machine in the back and a happy hour that keeps it honest.
perfect: you want a guided flight and a backyard pint
insider: Ask for a flight and let the bartenders pick; then grab a four-pack to go from the fridge on your way out.

name: Dba
pitch: An old-school 1st Ave beer bar with a chalkboard wall of taps, a deep whiskey shelf and a back garden that fills on warm afternoons. Open noon to 4 a.m. every day, dog-friendly, and there is a Nintendo Switch on the bar if the conversation runs out.
perfect: you want a serious beer list without the attitude
insider: Order the pickle martini, made with the bar's own brine, and ask the pint price up front since the receipt is not itemized.

name: Death & Co.
pitch: The East Village cocktail bar that wrote the book, literally, and still earns it: dark room, bow-tied bartenders and a menu that changes between a summer and a winter list. The drinks are the point; the snacks are fine but not why you are here.
perfect: a cocktail-focused date where the bartender guides you
insider: Arrive right at 6 p.m. opening and ask for a bar seat; tell the bartender what you like and let them go off menu.

name: Ding-A-Ling Bar
pitch: An Ave C bar open Wednesday through Saturday with resident DJs, sweet spritzes and martinis finished with candy garnishes, and a loose tiki-meets-Hong Kong look. Walking in on a Friday is easy, the room goes until 4 a.m., and the staff treat first-timers like regulars.
perfect: you want DJs and a martini without a line
insider: Wednesday is the night to go for the martinis; the bar is closed Sunday through Tuesday, so plan around it.

name: Dirt Candy
pitch: A vegetable tasting menu that converts meat eaters, five courses each built around a single vegetable, with a vegan version and cocktails that pick up the theme. Tips are included, the menu changes with the season and it is not cheap, so save it for an occasion.
perfect: an anniversary dinner that happens to be vegetarian
insider: Reservations go fast; watch for cancellations and take the chef's counter, where you can see dessert being plated.

name: Doc Holliday's
pitch: A roadhouse dive on Ave A that has not changed in thirty years: country on the jukebox, a pool table in back and bartenders who are not there to coddle you. It is loud and standing-room by late night, and the drinks are stronger than they are cheap.
perfect: you want a country jukebox and zero pretense
insider: Tip in cash on every round and you will get along fine with the bartenders; go before 9 p.m. if you want the pool table.

name: Donnybrook
pitch: A roomy Clinton St pub that changes with the clock: laptops and quiet pints on a weekday afternoon, games on the TVs by evening and a packed, dancing room on Friday and Saturday. The happy hour is one of the better deals on the Lower East Side and the bartenders are quick.
perfect: a cheap afternoon pint that turns into a night
insider: Tap-to-pay has not worked here, so bring a physical card or cash, and grab the sidewalk tables before dinner.

name: Double Down
pitch: The New York branch of the Las Vegas punk dive: stickers and graffiti on every surface, loud music, pool tables and some of the cheapest beer on Ave A. It is gritty on purpose and open noon to 4 a.m. every day, so it works for a snow-day afternoon as well as a last stop.
perfect: you want a two-dollar beer and loud punk
insider: Try the bacon martini the Vegas original is known for, bring a government ID that will pass a hard look, and head to the back patio.

name: Downtown social
pitch: A 2nd Ave sports bar with enough TVs that you will see your game, friendly servers who stick around through a packed soccer match and bar food that is fresher than it needs to be. On a quiet Sunday afternoon the sidewalk tables are an easy place for a few beers.
perfect: the match is on and you want a table
insider: Order the Caesar wrap with your beers; the kitchen does it well and it travels to the outdoor tables.

name: Dream baby
pitch: From the street it reads as a dim cocktail lounge with banquettes and candles, good for a weekday nightcap. Walk to the back and turn left and there is a second room with its own bar, a DJ and a disco ball spinning late 90s and 2000s hits on weekends.
perfect: you want to dance without a club line
insider: The cocktail list is written on the mirror behind the bar; the dance room in back is the move after 11 on Friday and Saturday.

name: Drom
pitch: A basement music venue on Ave A that books a global roster, from Nordic folk bands to jazz and hip-hop, with a sound system that outclasses the room. Eat before you come: the kitchen is an afterthought, a service charge is automatic and the aisles get tight once the show starts.
perfect: you want a seated show with a world-music lineup
insider: Eat beforehand and bring cash for the bar; a 20 percent service charge is added automatically and there is no tap water.

name: Drop Off Service/The Dancing Bull
pitch: A former laundromat on Ave A turned into the neighborhood's living room, all wood and brick, with a long craft draft list and a happy hour that has kept regulars for a decade. There is no kitchen, which is fine, because the point is a pint and a conversation that runs long.
perfect: a long, cheap afternoon pint with old friends
insider: Ask for the hand-pulled cask ale, and come early for the happy hour, when a gin and tonic runs about $7.

name: East 12th Osteria
pitch: A corner Italian at 12th and 1st with house-made pasta, a pistachio gnocchi people talk about and a habit of sending out limoncello or cannoli at the end of the meal. Service has had off nights recently, but the room is warm and it is easy to order several pastas and share.
perfect: a share-the-pastas dinner with a group
insider: Ask for the pasta as small plates so the table can taste three or four, and leave room for the free cannoli.

name: Eastpoint Bar
pitch: A polished sports bar on Ave B that packs out for Knicks games and still gets drinks and tacos to the table. There is a downstairs room that opens later for birthdays and late nights, and the staff are the reason regulars keep coming back.
perfect: a Knicks game with food that beats wings
insider: It is strictly 21 and over, even at the tables, so leave the younger friend at home; head downstairs after 11 on weekends.

name: El Camion
pitch: A cantina on Ave A for margaritas, guacamole and plates that arrive colorful and full, with a brunch that leans boozy. Eat in rather than ordering out; the takeout tacos have been rushed, but at the table the kitchen and servers pay attention.
perfect: a margarita brunch with a group on Ave A
insider: Order La Vampirita to drink and the esquites to start, and try the Coca-Cola braised carnitas as a main.

name: El Diablito
pitch: A tiny, bright taqueria on E 3rd St with about fifteen seats, a friendly counter and tacos that come out fast and oversized. The birria with consommé and the carne asada are the orders, and the price is a relief for the neighborhood.
perfect: a quick, cheap taco lunch near Tompkins
insider: Taco Tuesday gets you three hefty tacos for about $13; the first chip basket is free and the second is $2.

name: Eleven B
pitch: An old-school family pizzeria on Ave B that does a proper New York plain slice and the red-sauce Italian standards, pasta and chicken Marsala included. The regulars at the counter in back have been coming for years and will talk to anyone.
perfect: a plain slice and a side of neighborhood talk
insider: Order the plain slice at the counter and eat it in the little room in back with the regulars on a Saturday.

name: Elsa
pitch: A daytime spot on E 3rd St, open 10 to 4, built around enormous sage biscuits that stand in for the bun on sandwiches like avocado, bacon, fig jam and Swiss. There is outdoor seating and the Sunday brunch wait is usually short compared with the avenues.
perfect: a biscuit brunch without the Avenue B line
insider: Get the avocado and bacon biscuit sandwich; the fried chicken version comes buried in bacon, so ask for less if that is not your thing.

name: Empellon al pastor
pitch: A loud, order-at-the-bar taqueria on St Marks with murals on the walls and ceiling, drafts of beer, cider and wine, and a crowd that spills onto the sidewalk tables in summer. The nachos are the value play and feed a group; the tacos are good but priced like cocktails.
perfect: pre-game nachos and a draft on St Marks
insider: Happy hour is weekdays 4 to 7; the bacon-wrapped hot dog and the late-night breakfast burrito are the sleeper orders.

name: Empellon Cocina
pitch: The Empellón taqueria on West 4th St, with a front and back dining room, sidewalk tables and a chip order that arrives with a flight of seven salsas. The brussels sprout and fish tacos are small but dense with flavor, and the cucumber margarita is the drink.
perfect: a taco and margarita stop in the West Village
insider: Happy hour runs Monday to Friday, 5 to 7; start with chips and the seven salsas and use them on the tacos.

name: Ethos
pitch: A small plant and flower shop on Ave A that doubles as an incense, crystal and statue emporium, open 8 to 9 every day. Staff will build a succulent arrangement to your budget and tell you the price as they go, which is rarer than it should be.
perfect: you need a last-minute plant or bouquet on Ave A
insider: Ask them to assemble a succulent planter on the spot; pick the pot first and they price each piece as they add it.

name: Fish Bar
pitch: A tiny dive on E 5th St painted floor to ceiling with fish and sharks, dollar bills on the ceiling and rock on the speakers. A can of beer and a shot runs about $10, there is a special every day, and it goes from low-key afternoon to packed late night.
perfect: a ten-dollar beer-and-shot with longtime regulars
insider: Order the Kurt Cobain, the house drink, and take the daily special; Saturday opens at 2 p.m. for day drinking.

name: Fools Gold
pitch: A big, industrial-looking beer and whiskey bar on Houston with around thirty drafts, flights of both and a kitchen that does sliders, poutine and truffle fries well past midnight. The happy hour is a real deal and the staff stay fast even when it is wall to wall on a Friday.
perfect: a cheap happy hour before a night on Houston
insider: Order a beer flight and a whiskey flight to split, and try the smoked old fashioned; trivia is a weeknight draw.

name: Frankie's
pitch: A small old-school Italian on 2nd Ave with a big menu, homemade pasta and a sidewalk setup that is one of the nicer places to eat outside in warm weather. Service is friendly but can be uneven; the food, especially the mushroom tagliatelle, is the reason to go.
perfect: a sidewalk pasta dinner on a warm night
insider: Sit at the bar and let the bartender pick the wine; ask for a slice of lemon with the sausage pasta.

name: Giano
pitch: A warm Italian on E 7th St run by Italians who treat the room like a dinner party, with fresh pasta that leaves people saying it was the best they have had. Some find the seasoning heavy, but the ravioli in sage butter and the caprese are hard to argue with.
perfect: a dinner where the owners remember your face
insider: Order the spinach and ricotta ravioli in sage butter, and look at the dessert wine section of the list before the tiramisu.

name: Gomi Korean Wine Bar
pitch: A small, dim wine bar on Ave A whose owner grew up Korean in Brazil, so the plates run from kimchi dumplings to coxinhas and picanha, and the list has soju and sake alongside the wine. Sit at the bar and let him pour; the recommendations are the whole experience.
perfect: a date where someone else picks the wine
insider: Ask about oyster night and the happy hour fried chicken wings, and request the Brazilian hot sauce with the picanha.

name: Good night sonnys
pitch: A tile-floored cocktail and oyster bar on 1st Ave from the Wayland crew, open until 4 a.m. with a kitchen that keeps going late. The cocktails are the draw and the happy hour oysters are the deal, with the whipped codfish dip and clams casino as the supporting cast.
perfect: late oysters and a cocktail after the show
insider: Happy hour oysters have run about a dozen for $18; finish with the brown butter pecan bread pudding.

name: Grey Lady
pitch: A New England seafood shack transplanted to Delancey St, with dollar oysters every day until 7, including weekends, and a crab dip that is actually mostly crab. Service can lag when it is full, but the outdoor tables and the lobster mac make the wait easy.
perfect: dollar oysters on a weekend afternoon
insider: Wednesday is the night: half-price bottles of wine, $6 drafts and the dollar oysters, with a $20 burger and martini combo at the bar.

name: Gruppo
pitch: A bar-like neighborhood pizzeria on Ave B that does cracker-thin crust and lets you split a pie half and half. The Shroomtown, with three kinds of mushrooms, is the one people come back for, and the staff happily bring anchovies or extra cheese on the side.
perfect: a thin-crust pie and a glass of wine on B
insider: Order half Shroomtown, half sausage with caramelized onions, start with the Mediterranean salad and save room for the bread pudding.

name: Gyu-Kaku
pitch: The Cooper Square branch of the Japanese yakiniku chain, where you grill pork belly, kalbi and steak at the table and finish by toasting marshmallows over the coals. The all-you-can-eat option is the value move for a hungry group, and the hosts keep the room moving even when the entrance is mobbed.
perfect: a hands-on group dinner that ends with marshmallows
insider: Book ahead and go all-you-can-eat; the pork belly and the kalbi chuck rib are the cuts to load up on.

name: Hair of the dog
pitch: An Orchard St sports bar that is all screens by day and a packed, DJ-driven twenty-something party by Saturday night, with a kitchen that turns out better chicken tenders than it has any right to. The happy hour deals are strong; full-price rounds late on a weekend are not.
perfect: a match on every screen and a cheap happy hour
insider: Happy hour runs until 8 and includes weekends, when an espresso martini has gone for $7; sit by the Stanton St windows away from the bar.

name: Hasaki
pitch: An E 9th St sushi house that has been here since 1984, quiet and unhurried, where the counter omakase runs about $96 for twelve pieces, a hand roll, an appetizer and dessert. It is one of the better values in the neighborhood for this level of fish and a sure thing for an anniversary.
perfect: a calm anniversary omakase that will not break you
insider: Book the counter omakase with the chef; the kasugo and mackerel are the pieces to watch for, and yes, the toilet seat is heated.

name: Hawksmoor NYC (GRAMERCY)
pitch: The British steakhouse's New York home in a vaulted former ballroom on E 22nd St, where everything is cooked over charcoal and the rib-eye picks up a crust most steakhouses cannot match. It is far from the East Village and priced accordingly, but the service turns a birthday into an occasion.
perfect: a milestone birthday that calls for a proper steak
insider: Mention the celebration in your booking note, order the sticky toffee pudding, and look for the lunch set menu for a gentler bill.

name: Headless Widow
pitch: A rustic cocktail bar on 1st Ave with an Old Fashioned worth ordering, a happy hour that stretches it and a kitchen that does a flaky fish and chips and good mussels. Hosts can be firm about seating small parties at the bar when tables are empty, so ask nicely or come as a group.
perfect: a quiet cocktail and fish and chips midweek
insider: Order the fish and chips at the bar during happy hour; it is closed Mondays, and Saturday and Sunday open an hour earlier at 4.

name: Hearth Restaurant
pitch: A long-running Tuscan-American room at 12th and 1st with an open kitchen, warm sourdough with grass-fed butter and a roast half chicken that stays juicy, cooked without seed oils. Solo diners may be steered to the bar, which is honestly the better seat for watching the line.
perfect: a serious dinner that still feels like the neighborhood
insider: Order the variety burger, which does not look like much on the menu, and start with the focaccia and whipped ricotta.

name: Hekate Cafe & Elixir Bar
pitch: An alcohol-free bar on Ave B with a witchy, candlelit look, where the layered elixirs and mocktails are built with as much care as any cocktail across the street. There are teas for a cold afternoon, tarot readers on a sliding scale, a shelf of books to borrow and dogs under the tables.
perfect: a sober night out that still feels like one
insider: Tell the bartender what flavors you like and let them improvise; the Healer, with lavender and thyme, is the one to start with.

name: Holiday Cocktail Lounge
pitch: The St Marks dive that got a full makeover and kept the dive-y feel, with a long cocktail list, strong well drinks and a kitchen that turns out a very good pretzel. The catch is price: beer runs well over $10, so order a cocktail and treat it as a proper bar.
perfect: a good cocktail on St Marks without a reservation
insider: Skip the Guinness, which is priced like a cocktail, and ask the bartender for a Tiny Crusher; the pretzel is the snack.

name: Horus Cafe
pitch: An Egyptian cafe and hookah bar on Ave B, open until 4 a.m. every night, where servers actually stop to talk and the mezze and kebabs are better than the lounge setting suggests. Hookah smoke drifts through the room, so sit outside if that bothers you.
perfect: a late mezze plate and a hookah with friends
insider: Ask for a sidewalk table if you want to skip the smoke, and order the mezze spread to share before the kebabs.

name: Ichibantel
pitch: A dark Japanese comfort-food hall off 1st Ave, open until 3 a.m., where you walk through a tunnel into a room with anime playing on a projector. The katsu curry, karaage and chicken nanban are the orders, and it is one of the few real late-night kitchens around.
perfect: ramen or katsu curry at 2 in the morning
insider: Groups get an automatic 25 percent service charge even when sitting apart, so check the bill; the chicken nanban travels well as takeout.

name: Il Posto Accanto
pitch: A brick-walled Italian wine bar on E 2nd St run by an owner who is in the room and cooking, with a menu that changes with the market and pasta that is springy and light. Lunch is quiet and lovely; dinner fills with regulars who know to book.
perfect: a long, quiet Italian lunch on a weekday
insider: Ask them to hold a piece of lasagna when you reserve; it runs out, and the daily ragu is the other order.

name: International Bar
pitch: A narrow, no-frills dive on 1st Ave open 10 a.m. to 4 a.m., where the door is locked and buzzed open and the inside is nothing but cheap drinks, a good jukebox and talkative regulars. Service depends on who is behind the bar, which is part of the deal at a place like this.
perfect: a cheap whiskey chaser and a long argument
insider: If the door seems locked, wait a beat; the bartender buzzes you in, and the sidewalk seats out front are the best in the house.

name: Ippudo
pitch: The 4th Ave original of the tonkotsu ramen chain is still loud, still busy and still worth the wait for the rich broth and the pork buns. Expect to share a long communal table with strangers, and know that a group will not be seated until everyone has arrived.
perfect: a rich bowl of ramen on a cold night
insider: Order the Goma Q cucumbers and the karaage to start; arrive with your whole party, since incomplete groups wait outside.

name: Joe & Pat's NYC
pitch: A 1st Ave pizzeria built around a cracker-thin crust, where the tri pie splits marinara, vodka and pesto across one pie. It is crowded and loud in a good way and handles big groups, and there is a happy hour that runs on weekends too.
perfect: a thin-crust pie that a whole table will share
insider: Order the tri pie with the arugula salad and a lambrusco spritz; the cauliflower crust is surprisingly the sleeper.

name: Josie's Bar
pitch: A long-running E 6th St dive with a pool table, Buck Hunter and a jukebox, the kind of place to sit with a beer and talk to whoever is next to you. Fair warning: the staff and door can be brusque, so go in easy, order a drink first and do not expect a free water.
perfect: a midweek beer and a game of pool
insider: Buck Hunter and the pool table are the draw; water comes only with a drink order, so buy one before you ask.

name: Joyface
pitch: A 70s-styled disco bar on Ave C with plush couches, a disco ball and a dance floor that is the whole point: people come to dance, not to sit. The door is selective and gets tense on busy Saturdays, so go on a quieter night or early and the room is a joy.
perfect: you want to dance to disco, not stand around
insider: Arrive before 10 p.m. or go on a Sunday or Tuesday, when you walk right in; Saturday after 10:30 means a wait and a minimum.

name: Juke Bar
pitch: A small, dim cocktail bar on 2nd Ave with a backyard patio, a spicy margarita people keep ordering and sliders and truffle fries to go with it. It fills fast on weekend evenings, so a reservation or an early arrival makes the difference.
perfect: a backyard cocktail on a Thursday that runs late
insider: Book a table for weekend nights, ask for the patio, and try the lychee martini; Sunday brings a live band.

name: Kafana
pitch: A homey Serbian bistro on Ave C with brick walls, old photos and the feel of a family kitchen where people linger for hours over grilled meats and roasted peppers. It is small and popular, so reserve, and it is cash only, so stop at an ATM first.
perfect: a cold night calls for cevapi and red wine
insider: Order the cevapi and the braised lamb shank to share, ask for a Serbian red, and bring cash, since cards are not accepted.

name: Kanoyama Japanese Restaurant
pitch: A long-running 2nd Ave sushi house with larger-than-usual slices, a giant platter that feeds three and a counter omakase offered only two nights a week. The kitchen runs slow when takeout stacks up early, so sit down, order the fried vegetables and let the fish come.
perfect: a group sushi platter that is actually generous
insider: The omakase is only two nights a week and needs a reservation; the fried vegetables and chicken are the sleeper starters.

name: Karma Bar and Lounge NYC
pitch: A low-key hookah bar and lounge on 1st Ave where a beer and a shot at the end of the day costs what it should, the DJ keeps it moving and the staff are easy company. It is more chill than club, with sections you can claim for a group.
perfect: a cheap beer and shot before the night starts
insider: Happy hour runs until 8 p.m., so get there before then; a hookah has run about $20 with a small charge for fresh coals.

name: Karvouna Mezze
pitch: A relaxed Greek spot on the Bowery with a lounge up front, big portions and classic plates: hummus with a proper herb hit, a chicken gyro platter, grilled octopus with lemon potatoes. It is quiet early in the evening, which makes it a comfortable pre-show dinner.
perfect: an unhurried Greek dinner before a Bowery show
insider: Start with the spinach pie and the hummus; the portions are big enough that two mezze and one grill plate feeds two.

pitch: A hookah lounge on Avenue A where the music runs loud and late, with hummus and Middle Eastern plates to keep the table going. Service is warm when the room is slow, but ask about hookah and drink prices up front because the bill climbs fast.
perfect: you want hookah and loud music until 4 AM.
insider: Order the Love 66 hookah with mint and come on a Thursday for the dancehall sets.
name: Kazuza

pitch: A plain Irish sports bar at the bottom of Avenue A, heavy on hockey, Guinness, and Irish crisps, with a pool table in the basement. The bartenders can be brusque and the room shows its age, so treat it as a game-day stop rather than a night out.
perfect: the Rangers are on and you need a stool.
insider: The pool table is downstairs by the bathrooms and still takes quarters.
name: Kelly's Sports Bar

pitch: The 14th Street KFC is the fried chicken you can get at 2 in the morning, and that is the whole case for it. Counter staff are friendly enough but the kitchen is hot and harried, so check your box before you walk out.
perfect: it is 1 AM and only a drumstick will do.
insider: Order at the counter instead of online, where the sauces and drinks tend to get forgotten.
name: KFC

pitch: Three floors of Soviet kitsch on East 4th, with a theater downstairs, a red-curtained bar in the middle, and a louder, younger room up top. No cover, strong martinis around $17, and a crowd that skews a little older and a lot more literary than St Marks.
perfect: you want a reading, a martini, and red velvet.
insider: The theater on the ground floor charges about $20 for a show, but the bars upstairs have no cover.
name: KGB

pitch: A 30-year-old lounge at 1st and 1st with DJs on the weekends, a long happy hour, and bartenders who remember you after one visit. It gets very loud once the music starts, so come to dance or to sink into the couches in back, not to talk.
perfect: you want a cheap drink and a dance floor.
insider: There is no kitchen, but you can bring your own food in, so order a pizza nearby and carry it over.
name: La Linea

pitch: A roomy, colorful cantina on St Marks that is bigger inside than it looks, with fresh guacamole, strong salsas, and frozen margaritas in hibiscus and passionfruit. Bottomless brunch pours on the weaker side, so go for the food and the happy hour margs instead.
perfect: a group needs margaritas and a table without a wait.
insider: Marquita Tuesday is the night regulars show up for, and the chicken torta with red sauce is the sleeper order.
name: La Palapa

pitch: A plush, dimly lit vegan spot behind a small red door on 7th Street, where bao bun trios, kimchi mac and cheese, and corn ribs land as well with meat eaters as with vegans. Weekend brunch adds chilaquiles and chocolate chip pancakes, and the room fills by noon.
perfect: a vegetarian friend deserves the romantic table.
insider: Look for the small red door; the signage is easy to miss, and brunch walk-ins of three were seated without a wait.
name: Ladybird

pitch: A decades-old Tuscan trattoria on a quiet block of East 4th, with rigatoni cooked properly al dente, a wood-fired pizza, and servers who have been there forever. Portions are sized so two people can share a few plates, and it stays far from the St Marks crush.
perfect: you want pasta on a block nobody wanders down.
insider: The focaccia that arrives unasked is charged per person, so wave it off if you do not want it.
name: Lavagna

pitch: A tiny counter bistro on Orchard where the whole kitchen is in front of you and almost every seat is a date. The grilled octopus, hanger steak with gratin, and chickpea pancake are the orders, and the room is loud and tight in the best way.
perfect: two of you want Paris without a reservation.
insider: Get in line around 4:45 on a weekend for the 5:30 open; later arrivals leave a number and get called back.
name: Le French Diner

pitch: The tiki room under Niagara on the corner of 7th and A, with a dance floor, a photo booth, and a happy hour that runs until 8. The music and the crowd are the draw; the bartenders can be curt about ordering and tipping, so keep a round going.
perfect: you want to dance on Avenue A before midnight.
insider: The photo booth in back takes $10, and you are expected to keep ordering if you hold a table.
name: Lei Bar

pitch: A warm saloon on 3rd Ave that doubles as the neighborhood's party room, with a long beer list, sliders people go back for thirds of, and sidewalk tables with their own TVs. Entrees run past $20, but the 4 to 8 happy hour brings wine and mixed drinks down to about $8.
perfect: a big game and a sidewalk seat line up.
insider: The sidewalk seating has TVs, so you can watch the game outside, and the staff will drag over extra chairs.
name: Linen Hall

pitch: A friendly bar on 2nd Ave with a Victorian-meets-mugshots look, a $7 cocktail of the week, and a kitchen that takes its truffle fries and chicken sandwich seriously. The servers and bartenders are the reason people come back, so sit at the bar and talk.
perfect: happy hour with coworkers needs real food too.
insider: The cocktail of the week is $7, and the semi-private room upstairs takes groups of 35 or so.
name: Little Rebel

pitch: The Bowery Hotel's lobby is a wood-paneled, candlelit living room where the cocktails are impeccable and the people-watching includes the occasional celebrity. Service treats a walk-in drinker like a guest, and the outdoor lounge is the place to be when the weather allows.
perfect: you want one expensive, perfect cocktail in old New York.
insider: Come for a couple of cocktails in the lobby; you do not need a room key to sit down.
name: Lobby Bar @ Bowery Hotel

pitch: A low-lit cocktail bar on 7th Street with a few connected rooms, a speakeasy feel, and drinks like the floral Astral Plane and the smooth Handsome Devil. Weekends it packs with a college-age crowd and seats vanish, so come early or midweek.
perfect: you want cocktails underground before the crowd arrives.
insider: Happy hour is 5 to 7, which is also the only window with seats; after 10 on weekends expect a wait and a strict door.
name: Lovers of Today

pitch: A classic, cramped French bistro at 1st and 1st that has been doing steak frites, escargots, and profiteroles the same way for decades. Tables sit elbow to elbow and service can stretch when it is full, which is most nights, so book ahead.
perfect: you want steak au poivre at midnight.
insider: Book a table; the bar is too tight to wait at comfortably, and skip the tarte tatin for the profiteroles.
name: Lucien

pitch: A ten-year-old dive across from Tompkins Square with cheap beer-and-shot combos, a good jukebox, and a backyard with a swing. The bartenders are quick and friendly, and a burger and fries will run you under $20, which is rare on this block.
perfect: you want a backyard beer across from the park.
insider: Grab the swing on the back patio during happy hour; bar seats are tight, and lingering without ordering is frowned on.
name: Lucky

pitch: Lucy's is the Avenue A dive with the pool tables, the jukebox, and a name that has meant something on this block for decades. Lately the door and the bartenders have a reputation for favoring regulars, so arrive easygoing and do not expect a warm welcome.
perfect: you want pool and a jukebox, not conversation.
insider: The pool tables are the reason to come, but they are sometimes locked, so ask before you settle in.
name: Lucys

pitch: A roomy sports bar on 1st Ave with TVs wrapped around the back room, a pool table, a photo booth, and a real menu of oversized burgers and wings. On fall Saturdays it is the Ohio State bar in Manhattan, so plan around that if scarlet is not your color.
perfect: your group wants a game, wings, and elbow room.
insider: Tuesday trivia comes with two snacks for $15 and $8 happy hour drinks; the snacks are full meals.
name: Lydia's

pitch: A small brick-walled cocktail bar off 6th Ave where every drink is built around a spice, from the bourbon-based Vanilla to a savory gin Basil with tomato notes. Happy hour brings $12 cocktails and $2 oysters, but the oysters can take a while, so order them first.
perfect: you want a cocktail menu that reads like a spice rack.
insider: Order the oysters the moment you sit down at happy hour, and ask for the namesake Mace cocktail.
name: Mace

pitch: A minimalist bar facing Tompkins Square that serves tinned fish, perfectly toasted bread, and cheap beer, with trivia, karaoke, and watch parties through the week. Bring the dog and sit outside, and be ready for a tip screen that starts at 20 percent.
perfect: you want tinned fish and a park-facing seat.
insider: Order a tin, the bread, and a spiked coconut water for the outside tables on a summer afternoon.
name: Maiden Lane

pitch: A no-frills Avenue B dive with Buck Hunter, trivia nights, a good playlist, and bartenders who improvise cocktails when the back bar runs short. It is the kind of place you come for one and stay through the game.
perfect: you want trivia and a pickleback without pretense.
insider: Trivia night hands the losing team a free shot, and the bartenders will build you a cocktail off-menu.
name: Mama's Bar

pitch: A laid-back Rivington corner bar that has lasted 20 years on good taps, rock on the jukebox, and clean bathrooms. It is beer and wine with a few sakes and a solid non-alcoholic beer, and it is quiet enough on weeknights to read a book at the bar.
perfect: you want a serious beer list and no scene.
insider: The happy hour pours a Firestone Walker for about $6, and the little sake cartons are worth a look.
name: Marshall Stack

pitch: A lively French spot on St Marks with a terrace, live singers who move from Mexican to Greek standards, and a room that ends up dancing. The food holds up, with a proper chicken cordon bleu, onion soup, mussels, and a French toast worth a brunch trip.
perfect: dinner should turn into singing and plate-breaking.
insider: The DJ comes on after 10:45 and the bar packs out, so book dinner early if you want to hear yourself.
name: MARY LOUS

pitch: A dark, gothic little mezcal bar on 6th Street with flights, a long list of smoky cocktails, and an owner who takes care of the room. Non-drinkers get a real mango margarita without the booze, and the upstairs nook is where you want to be on a cold night.
perfect: you want a mezcal flight in candlelight.
insider: Ask for the upstairs nook, and come on a weekend when the live music is playing.
name: Mayamezcal

pitch: Southern Thai cooking on 1st Street that is salt-forward, herb-heavy, and properly spicy, with a cocktail list that keeps up. Minced pork with a crispy egg, massaman with roti, and the raw marinated shrimp are the orders, and dinner lands around $30 a head.
perfect: you want Thai food that does not pull punches.
insider: Order the kra prow with the fried egg on top and the roti with curry; portions run small, so get extra.
name: MayRee

pitch: The oldest saloon in the neighborhood still pours exactly two things, light ale and dark ale, two mugs at a time onto a sawdust floor. It is packed with tourists and regulars alike, the food is a burger and a hot dog, and none of that matters.
perfect: someone visiting needs to see old New York.
insider: Cash only, and ordering a round means two small mugs per person; try the dark.
name: McSorley's Old Ale House

pitch: A small standing-room venue on Houston that has broken in indie bands since the nineties, with a sound system much better than the size suggests. There is a bar up front, benches along the walls, and no food, so eat first and get there for the opener.
perfect: you want to be ten feet from the band.
insider: Stand right up front; it is not too loud even there, and the back fills early on sold-out nights.
name: Mercury Lounge

pitch: A bright Jamaican beach shack on Avenue A with fall-off-the-bone jerk chicken, coconut rice and peas, caramelized plantains, and a rum punch that hits harder than it tastes. Weekend DJs play dancehall and reggae, and the happy hour drops cocktails to about $8.
perfect: you want jerk chicken and a rum punch outside.
insider: Come for happy hour and get the plantains and oxtail spring rolls; the cod fritters divide people.
name: Miss Lilies 7A Cafe

pitch: A playful, tiled cocktail bar on 1st Ave with drinks named like jokes, from a frozen Painkiller to a matcha McFloozy, plus dumplings and crispy rice to soak them up. The staff are fast and upbeat, and happy hour runs every night they are open.
perfect: you want cocktails that are fun on purpose.
insider: Order the cosmo and the French fries, and hit the happy hour, which runs every night they are open.
name: Mister Paradise

pitch: A long, narrow Alphabet City dive with a pool table in the back room, Skee-Ball, a good Guinness pour, and live bluegrass and jazz that are far better than a bar this cheap should have. The staff are busy and no-frills, and they expect a tip on every round.
perfect: you want live bluegrass and a cheap pint.
insider: The bluegrass jam starts at 9 on Sunday nights and jazz takes Tuesdays at 9; the pool table is through the back room.
name: Mona's

pitch: A Korean fried chicken spot on 4th Street dressed like a jazz library, with a wall of records spinning overhead and flowers everywhere. The wings, cabbage pancake, and crispy chicken rolls are the safe orders; the galbi jjim and porridge have let people down for the price.
perfect: the table cares as much about the room as the food.
insider: Stick to the wings and the baechu jeon, and ask for a seat near the record wall.
name: Mono+Mono

pitch: A retro, disco-ball-in-the-bathroom bar on Avenue A that does a $25 bottomless brunch where you pick your drink, not just mimosas. It gets loud enough that conversation is work, but the staff are generous and the eggs Benedict with salmon is better than it needs to be.
perfect: bottomless brunch should be cheap and loud.
insider: Bottomless is 90 minutes for $25 and any drink counts; get the Benedict with salmon and skip the burrito.
name: Motel No tell
Motorino East Village
pitch: Wood-fired Neapolitan pies with properly blistered crusts, two minutes in a 950-degree oven, and the Brussels sprout and clam pizzas are still the ones people come back for. It is the rare East Village pizza place where a last-minute Friday table is realistic, and the servers are genuinely warm.
perfect: you want real Neapolitan pizza without a long wait
insider: The mortadella and burrata pie eats like a hero, and breaking the burrata over the slices is the move.

name: Nai Tapas Bar
pitch: Spanish regulars say this is the closest New York gets to home: croquettes like a grandmother's, a fideuà worth building the meal around, and a flan to finish. The room is handsome, service goes out of its way, and the front corner handles a table of eight or a rehearsal dinner of twenty.
perfect: a group dinner that needs to feel like a party
insider: Order the fideuà and the curry chickpeas, and ask how they build the Filipino Cover Band cocktail.

name: Nexus
pitch: This is the basement lounge under One and One, where the long Irish bar upstairs turns into a no-cover dance floor on weekend nights. The crowd skews early twenties and fresh out of school, and both floors are packed by midnight.
perfect: your early-twenties friends want to dance without paying cover
insider: It opens at 8 on Fridays and Saturdays and runs until 4, and there is no cover to get downstairs.

name: Nowhere Bar
pitch: A low-ceilinged, below-ground gay dive on 14th Street, lit mostly by disco ball, with cheap, well-made drinks, a jukebox, and a pool table you have to shake to wake up. It is packed wall to wall most nights, a cover sometimes appears, and the bartenders expect a tip with every round.
perfect: you want a dark, unfussy gay bar with no pretense
insider: Bring cash: drinks are cheap for the city and tipping in cash keeps the bartenders on your side.

name: Nowon
pitch: Korean-American gastropub on 6th Street with a loud, dim, R&B-scored room and a menu that keeps changing, anchored by the famous cheeseburger and the ricotta toast. The seven-course Classic Mixtape at $52 is the way to go with a group, and the staff keep plates moving and the table clear.
perfect: a loud, fun group dinner with a tasting menu
insider: Regulars split on the famous cheeseburger, so the truffle steak burger and the honey tots are the safer picks.

name: Nublu (New One)
pitch: The Avenue C club with a center-of-the-room stage, its own record label, and a gorgeous lit interior lined with images of Black music legends, booking jazz, disco nights, and whatever else fits. Producer Mondays is the thing to see, a chaotic, crowded jam that regulars call the best musical night of their week.
perfect: you want live music that is actually adventurous
insider: Come on a Monday for Producer Mondays, pay the entry fee, and know the water is free if you are not drinking.

name: Nuyorican Poets Cafe
pitch: The storied Loisaida poetry slam room, decades on, where spoken word artists bare their souls to a packed crowd for a cheap ticket. The bar is just wine, beer, and soft drinks, seats are first come, and doors can open late, so line up early.
perfect: you want a Friday night poetry slam
insider: Buy tickets online ahead of the Friday slam and grab a seat at the bar when the doors open.

name: Omar's Kitchen & Rum Bar
pitch: A small, colorful Jamaican kitchen and rum bar on Clinton Street, six years in, where the curried oxtail, saltfish fritters, and jerk chicken gnocchi come out with real flavor and big portions. The cocktails are the other half of the draw: tamarind, sorrel, rum punches, and a shaken piña colada, with a DJ some nights.
perfect: a lively dinner with rum cocktails and oxtail
insider: Order the tamarind cocktail and the oxtail, and pick the fritters over the wings.

name: One and One
pitch: A big, multi-level Irish sports bar at 1st and Houston with game screens, mini corn dogs, a long happy hour, and a dance lounge downstairs on weekends. Omar the manager is why people throw birthdays here, though on a packed World Cup afternoon the room runs hot and the kitchen lags.
perfect: you need seats for a big match
insider: The Cobb salad is a sleeper, and the mini corn dogs are the bar snack to order with a pint.

name: Otto’s Shrunken Head
pitch: The neighborhood's rock-and-roll tiki bar on far 14th Street, with glowing tiki mugs, a vintage photo booth, and rockabilly, ska, and punk bands in the back room. Longtime regulars grumble that the drinks got pricey and the punk edge softened, so come for the music and the room more than the cocktails.
perfect: a rockabilly night with a flaming volcano bowl
insider: Check the calendar for Subway to Skaville, the ska and rocksteady night, and eat beforehand since there is no food.

name: Pangea
pitch: A low-key Italian-Mediterranean restaurant on 2nd Avenue with a tight, intimate cabaret room in the back that books real downtown performers. The food is simple and fine rather than the point, so eat early and treat dinner as the opening act.
perfect: dinner and a cabaret show in one stop
insider: Book the show and arrive early enough to finish dinner before it starts, since the room is small and shows begin on time.

name: Panna II Garden Indian Restaurant
pitch: The chili-pepper-light-draped Indian restaurant on 1st Avenue that just had its movie moment, still cheap, still packed, and still handing out complimentary ice cream after a spicy meal. The room is sensory overload, the tables are tight, and the owner's recommendations are worth taking.
perfect: you want cheap, loud, over-the-top Indian dinner
insider: It is cash or Venmo only, you bring your own beer, and the samosas and paneer are the dishes to start with.

name: Paquito's
pitch: A no-frills 1st Avenue Mexican counter that has been turning out oversized burritos and tacos since the mid-nineties, guacamole included in the price and a mean hot sauce on the side. The food is consistently good and cheap for the neighborhood, but the counter service can be distracted, so check your order and state any allergy twice.
perfect: a huge burrito on the cheap, late
insider: Get the shrimp burrito, which comes with guacamole and a small salad at no extra charge.

name: Pardon my French
pitch: A cozy retro bistro on Avenue B that locals keep coming back to for the escargot, bone marrow, mussels with a mountain of fries, and duck confit. The dining room gets loud and the steak is the weak spot, so sit in the back garden or at the bar and order everything else.
perfect: a French bistro dinner with a garden
insider: Ask for the back garden in warm weather, and get the moules marinières for the fries alone.

name: Paul's Palace
pitch: The old-school 2nd Avenue burger joint, kitschy decor and all, that serves giant hand-formed burgers and steak fries at fair prices with quick, no-fuss service. In a smash-burger world it is the last of its kind, and regulars have been coming since the nineties for exactly that reason.
perfect: you want a huge classic burger, no frills
insider: It is cash only, the steak fries are the right side, and the oversized burger sign outside is the photo.

name: PDT (Please Don't Tell)
pitch: The speakeasy you enter through the phone booth inside Crif Dogs, still dark, still booked up, still mixing creative cocktails you can pair with a hot dog and tater tots. The hostess may quote a long wait even when the room is quiet, so reserve ahead rather than winging it.
perfect: a first date that needs a party trick
insider: Reserve in advance, ask for the little corner booth, and try the Cha Nom Thai.

name: Petite Boucherie
pitch: The small corner outpost of Boucherie at Christopher and Gay Street, with big windows, an open kitchen, and the same Paris-postcard feel at a gentler scale. Steak frites, onion soup, and the roast chicken are the orders, and the bartenders will match a cocktail to your plate.
perfect: a date night that wants a Paris stand-in
insider: Sit at the bar and let the bartender pair a cocktail, and know the chicken is the sleeper hit.

name: Phebe's Tavern & Grill
pitch: A Bowery institution since the sixties, a big casual bar and grill where the fish and chips, French onion soup, and fries come in cheaper than most diners and the Guinness is poured right. Game nights and weekends get young and rowdy, so for a quiet meal go on a weekday afternoon.
perfect: a cheap, filling meal near Astor Place with a game on
insider: Dogs are welcome, and the French onion soup and natural-cut fries are the orders at the bar.

name: Phoenix
pitch: A relaxed gay and lesbian mainstay on 13th Street with a jukebox, a good events calendar, and Sunday live music with free barbecue in the summer. The bartenders range from generous to chilly depending on the night, and there is a card minimum, so bring cash.
perfect: a Sunday afternoon with music and free barbecue
insider: There is a twenty-dollar card minimum and the ATM is unreliable, so arrive with cash.

name: Pineapple Club
pitch: A sprawling two-floor tropical cocktail bar on 6th Street where the inventive drinks, like a clarified cucumber martini or a beet cocktail, outshine a hit-or-miss food menu. The front upstairs gets crushed, so push toward the back where there is room and the bartenders come to you.
perfect: fun cocktails with a group before going out
insider: Stick to the oysters and bao on the food side, and expect to be hurried along during happy hour.

name: Plado
pitch: A warm Mediterranean tasting bar on 2nd Street built for sharing rounds of small plates, with a seasonal menu, taro gnocchi, short rib that falls apart, and staff who handle allergies carefully. Seasoning can run shy, so ask for salt without guilt, and the Italy-versus-Spain cheese board is the right opener.
perfect: a birthday dinner that can share everything
insider: Start with the Italy versus Spain board with burrata and follow with the short rib.

name: Planet Rose
pitch: The red-walled, zebra-seated karaoke dive on Avenue A where the main room sings together, you pay a couple of dollars a song, and Missy behind the bar remembers you a year later. The private room is a steal for groups, with house liquor included, and it is open until 4 every night.
perfect: ten friends need a karaoke room with booze included
insider: Book the private room through Missy for groups, or just hand in a song code at the bar and wait for your name.

name: Poco
pitch: A loud, big-windowed Avenue B brunch spot where the draw is bottomless mimosas and sangria pitchers, refilled fast, more than the Spanish-leaning plates. The French toast and hash browns are the plates to order, and check drink prices before you commit, since the bill can run higher than the menu suggests.
perfect: a boozy brunch that is about the drinks
insider: The bottomless deal is worth it because refills actually arrive, and the French toast is the plate to get.

name: Populares Mexican Restaurant
pitch: A modern, artsy Mexican spot on Avenue B that stays late, with spicy margaritas, mezcal chicken, warm churros, and a tres leches French toast at brunch. Service is sweet but slow on drinks, so settle in and order the next round early.
perfect: a late dinner with good margaritas
insider: Order the mezcal chicken, ask the bartender for a drink recommendation, and save room for the churros.

name: Pretty Ricky's
pitch: A roomy Rivington Street neighborhood bar with photo-covered walls, a back room with windows open to the street, a big craft beer list, and one of the better happy hours in the area. The burger and oysters are solid, and the bartenders treat walk-ins like regulars.
perfect: a cheap happy hour that does not feel cheap
insider: Happy hour has an espresso martini on tap for seven dollars, and drinks can lag the food, so order a round early.

name: Proletariat
pitch: A tiny, raucous craft beer bar on St Marks Place with a rare, rotating list on the wall, smaller pours so you can try more, and a knowledgeable bartender instead of table service. There is a vegan, British-leaning kitchen too, and the rarebit is the plate to get.
perfect: beer nerds want something rare without a reservation
insider: Ask for half pours to work through the list, and order the rarebit.

name: Punjabi
pitch: The East Houston counter where cab drivers and locals have eaten for decades: pick two numbered vegetarian dishes from the steam table for about eight dollars, get them over rice, and eat standing up. It is homey, not oily, and very cheap, and the saag and the samosa chaat are the ones to pick.
perfect: a cheap, fast, homecooked vegetarian lunch
insider: Point at the numbers you want, confirm the price before you pay, and get the saag and the bread pakora.

name: Pylos
pitch: A snug, long 7th Street Greek room under a ceiling of hanging clay pots, where the grilled octopus, dolmades in lemon sauce, and sesame-crusted baked feta with marmalade are the dishes people dream about afterward. Tables are close and prices run above the usual Greek spot, so it works best as a date.
perfect: a Greek date night with wine
insider: Sit at the bar if you have no reservation, and order the octopus and the dolmades.

name: Rebel
pitch: A rustic, intimate Haitian restaurant and lounge on Clinton Street with griyo, soup joumou, stewed goat, black rice, and cocktails strong enough to transport you. A DJ plays in the evenings, service is friendly if blunt, and a Wednesday walk-in is easy.
perfect: you want real Haitian food and a late-night lounge
insider: Order the griyo with a side of rice, the Creole wings, and the lemon drop martini from the bar.

name: Remedy
pitch: A 24-hour East Houston diner that has outlived most of its kind, with huge portions, a sprawling menu, chicken and waffles, turkey bacon, a tuna melt, and a window seat on the street at three in the morning. Staff are warm but can rush you, and the weekend brunch is a fixed price with a drink included.
perfect: you need breakfast at three in the morning
insider: The rigatoni alla vodka and the French onion soup are the late-night orders, and the window tables face Houston.

name: Rosella
pitch: An Avenue A sushi counter that sources locally and bends the rules, with a house soy sauce, inventive crudo, a fish sausage slider, and a carrot cake that gets mentioned alongside the omakase. Service is the kind that notices you over-ordered and says so, and sitting at the counter turns dinner into a show.
perfect: a celebratory sushi dinner that is not traditional
insider: Book the sushi counter, order the miso soup to start, and leave room for the carrot cake.

name: Rosie's Mexican Restaurant
pitch: A big, bustling Mexican restaurant on 2nd Street where the hand-pressed tortillas are made from Oaxacan maize, the margaritas are some of the city's best, and the staff treat regulars and first-timers the same. Portions of rice and beans run small for the prices, so lean on happy hour and the tacos.
perfect: a margarita-first group dinner on a weekend
insider: Sit at the bar for happy hour, where the quesadilla is four dollars, and order the seasonal watermelon margarita.

name: Royale
pitch: The Avenue C neighborhood bar and burger joint with a year-round patio, a well-made cocktail list, and a classic burger that regulars prefer to the smash version. It is quiet on a winter Monday and a Knicks-game madhouse in the spring, with a happy hour that holds either way.
perfect: a patio burger and a cocktail, late
insider: Order the classic Royale burger over the smash burger and let Maya or DJ mix your drink.

name: Saint
pitch: A brick-walled brasserie on 2nd Ave with a secret garden room and a speakeasy tucked behind it, which is why half the neighborhood seems to book birthdays here. Come for cocktails and the octopus starter rather than the burger, and expect the bar to move slowly when private parties fill the back.
perfect: you need a room for a birthday dinner.
insider: Ask to see the speakeasy before a private event takes it over for the night.

name: Sake Bar Decibel
pitch: A basement sake bar on 9th St that feels lifted out of Osaka, loud and scuffed and papered in graffiti, with a sake list long enough to get lost in. Order by the glass and let the servers steer you, and know that on a busy night the staff push tables to drink up and turn over.
perfect: you want a loud, low-ceilinged sake crawl for two.
insider: Pairs get seated far faster than groups of four, so go as a duo and skip the trios in favor of single glasses.

name: Sake Bar Satsko
pitch: A tiny izakaya on 7th St where the staff are loose and loud, the sake pours are generous and you tend to leave with a new friend or two. The food comes out slowly and recent nights have been unpredictable, so treat it as a drinking stop with snacks rather than dinner.
perfect: you want a rowdy sake nightcap with strangers.
insider: Order the karaage and squid as soon as you sit down, because the curry rice takes a while.

name: San Loco
pitch: Hard-shell gringo-Mex tacos and strong margaritas on Avenue C, open until midnight most nights and until 2 AM on Fridays and Saturdays. Nobody comes for refined food, but the queso loco tacos and a pitcher have kept regulars loyal for a decade.
perfect: it is late and you want cheesy tacos and margaritas.
insider: You order at the counter before sitting down, even though the room looks like a sit-down restaurant.

name: San Marzano
pitch: Handmade pasta in a cozy, art-filled room on 2nd Ave where a full plate still lands around twenty-five dollars, which is why it is packed every weekend. Pick a shape, pick a sauce, add the burrata, and expect noise when the room is full.
perfect: you want real pasta without a fifty-dollar check.
insider: Weekend brunch comes with bottomless mimosas, and the vodka rigatoni is the dish people come back for.

name: Scratchers
pitch: An Irish dive on 5th St between 2nd and 3rd with wooden benches, fairy lights, a UK-heavy playlist and bartenders who notice you even when it is three deep. Cheap drinks and a proper Guinness make it a reliable last stop or bar-crawl waypoint.
perfect: you want a Guinness and a nightcap without fuss.
insider: Tuesday and Wednesday nights are the quiet ones, and nobody minds if you bring a pizza in.

name: SenYa
pitch: A small, minimalist Japanese room on 1st Ave with six or so tables and a kitchen that likes a twist, from foie gras sushi to a snow crab mazemen with bone marrow. It is not cheap, so the restaurant week set is the move if you catch it.
perfect: you want inventive sushi and have a budget.
insider: The bone marrow melts on the tongue and the uni is the sushi to try, though it runs a little bitter.

name: Sing Sing
