pitch: Private karaoke rooms on Avenue A with a huge song list, open until 4 AM every night, and a staff that is friendly when the place is not slammed. On busy weekends the room service button goes unanswered and you end up fetching your own drinks from a crowded bar.
perfect: your group wants to scream-sing until 4 AM.
insider: Order buckets of beer for the whole room at once, since single drink orders tend to arrive wrong or late.

name: Sing Sing Karaoke
pitch: The St Marks branch of the private-room karaoke chain, open 6 PM to 4 AM every night with a broad song list in a brick building. Recent visits report surprise room charges and a brusque door, so get the all-in price in writing before you sing.
perfect: you want karaoke on St Marks and will haggle first.
insider: The sign out front advertises a per-person room rate, so confirm exactly what it covers before handing over ID.

name: Slainte
pitch: A big, brick-walled Irish sports bar on the Bowery with a long beer list, soccer and basketball on every screen, and pub food that is better than it needs to be. The nachos, sliders and even the steak get real praise, and the bartenders stay kind when March Madness packs the floor.
perfect: you need a game on and real food.
insider: Doors open at noon daily and 11 AM on weekends, so it works for early kickoffs.

name: Sly Fox
pitch: A true dive on 2nd Ave with Chucky and his bride behind the bar, rock on the speakers, a Ukrainian streak and shots cheap enough to raise an eyebrow. The crowd skews older and regular, bartenders remember faces for years, and nobody is making you a craft cocktail.
perfect: you want a four-dollar shot and loud rock.
insider: It is closed Sundays and Mondays and opens at 6 PM the rest of the week, so it is a night bar only.

name: Soba-ya
pitch: A calm, Michelin-recognized noodle house on 9th St that makes its own soba and udon, served hot or cold with seasonal specials like chilled soba under fresh uni. The entrance alone feels like a flight to Japan, and the broth tastes like someone's home cooking.
perfect: you want quiet, handmade noodles at lunch.
insider: Try the kamo nanban duck soba or the zaru soba, and look for the seasonal specials board.

name: Socarrat
pitch: The Nolita paella bar, a short walk below Houston, where the rice comes with a proper crisp socarrat bottom and the gambas al ajillo are worth the trip alone. Paella is priced per person with a two-serving minimum, so bring company or stick to tapas if you are solo.
perfect: you want paella and live flamenco on a Tuesday.
insider: Tuesday nights bring live Spanish music and a flamenco dancer, and the kitchen handles gluten-free paella well.

name: Soda Club
pitch: A dim, candlelit vegan Italian spot on Avenue B doing handmade pasta, Roman-style pizza and natural wines, and most people never notice the vegan part. Opinions on the pasta split, but the focaccia, the pistachio rotini and the wine service get consistent love.
perfect: you want natural wine and pasta that happens to be vegan.
insider: Sit at the bar, where the bartender will pour tastes of a few wines before you commit to a glass.

name: Soho Diner NYC
pitch: A retro diner inside the SoHo Grand with yellow globe lights, booths and a jukebox, open from 7 AM to midnight and until 2 AM on weekends. The vegan burger and banana pancakes win fans, but the kitchen is uneven and the prices are hotel prices, so go for the room and the late hours.
perfect: it is 1 AM in SoHo and you want fries.
insider: The vegan banana pancakes and vegan burger are the safe orders, and they will swap hash browns for fries.

name: Solas
pitch: A two-floor bar on 9th St with a packed ground floor and a dark upstairs lounge where a DJ keeps people dancing until 4 AM on weekends. The Wednesday salsa party has run for sixteen years, and the bouncers have a short fuse, so keep your approach polite.
perfect: you want to dance in the East Village on a Wednesday.
insider: Wednesday salsa night is fifteen dollars at the door and includes a lesson if you arrive early.

name: Soothr
pitch: A Michelin-recognized Thai restaurant on 13th St whose duck noodles, chicken khao soi and yum nuer taste like someone's mother cooked them, served in a packed, loud room that runs like clockwork. Food arrives almost as soon as you order, which is good because tables are capped at ninety minutes.
perfect: you want the best Thai dinner nearby, fast.
insider: Tables have a ninety-minute limit, and the chicken khao soi runs hotter than the rest of the menu.

name: Sophie's
pitch: A no-frills Alphabet City barroom with a pool table, a jukebox and cheap drinks, holding out against everything that has changed around it. The longtime bartender runs the room her way and recent visitors have clashed with her, so follow the house rules and you will be fine.
perfect: you want to shoot pool until 4 AM.
insider: One person in the bathroom at a time, and the pool table is the reason regulars keep coming back.

name: Spikes
pitch: A corner dive at 14th and A with darts, a few TVs for sports, a TouchTunes jukebox and bartenders who are quick with a pour. The energy is frenetic and the staff can be prickly, so it suits a loud group more than a quiet solo drink.
perfect: your crew wants darts and a game, no frills.
insider: There is no kitchen but you can bring food in, and it opens at noon every day.

name: St. Dymphna’s
pitch: A snug Irish pub on St Marks with a back room and a patio, weekend happy hour and a door guy who keeps the line civil when the weather turns warm. Check your bill before tipping, because gratuity is sometimes added automatically and the screen will still ask for more.
perfect: you want a pint and a patio on St Marks.
insider: A twenty percent gratuity is often already on the tab, so skip the extra prompt on the card reader.

name: Standings
pitch: A tiny pennant-lined sports bar on 7th St with a dozen taps, ten small TVs, about ten stools and a crowd that actually watches the game. It is a Mets bar at heart, the owner works the room, and you can order in food since the bar has none.
perfect: you want to watch the game with real fans.
insider: Cards are Visa or Mastercard only with a fifteen-dollar minimum, and weeknight games are far quieter than Saturdays.

name: Stickett Inn
pitch: A small, pretty bar on 1st Ave built around its own house-made cider, dry rather than sweet and poured by an owner who makes you feel like a regular. Recent visits have been uneven, with warm cider and so-so cocktails reported, so order the cider on a good night and keep it simple.
perfect: you want cider instead of beer and a quiet corner.
insider: The cider is the point here, and the restroom is prettier than most bars' front rooms.

name: Suki
pitch: All-you-can-eat sushi on 1st Ave ordered from an iPad, with sashimi, nigiri, pork buns and hot dishes like roasted fish collar included in one price. The menu leans heavily on salmon, so mix in the galbi and beef-wrapped enoki before your palate gives out.
perfect: you want to overeat sushi for sixty dollars.
insider: Arrive around 6 PM on a weekday for an empty room, because a line forms by eight.

name: Supper
pitch: A candlelit, rustic Northern Italian trattoria on 2nd St with an open kitchen, complimentary bread with white beans in olive oil, and a tagliatelle al ragù people plan whole evenings around. It is cash only, with an ATM inside, and the chicken parm has a following of its own.
perfect: you want a slow, candlelit pasta dinner and have cash.
insider: Cash only, so hit the ATM by the door, and do not skip the marinated white beans that arrive with the bread.

name: Taverna Di Bacco
pitch: A brick-walled Italian bistro on Ludlow where chef Maurizio greets the room himself, brings out dishes and will sit down for a chat if you let him. The five-course chef's option is the way to go, the chocolate mousse ends the night, and reservations matter on weekends.
perfect: you want the chef at your table and a long dinner.
insider: Ask for the chef's five-course menu, and arrive mid-afternoon on a weekend to skip the reservation scramble.

name: Taverna Kyclades East Village
pitch: The East Village outpost of the Astoria Greek seafood institution, an airy room with an open kitchen, big portions and grilled shrimp that arrive juicy and charred. Ownership has changed and the fish can run oily, so stick to the grilled seafood, spreads with warm pita and the lemon potatoes.
perfect: you want grilled fish and Greek portions without a wait.
insider: A non-cash surcharge of a few percent lands on card bills, so bring cash if that bothers you.

name: Ten Degrees
pitch: A loud, upbeat wine and cocktail bar on St Marks with a long happy hour, a back room that books out for birthdays and a hands-on owner named Aaron. Weekends go standing-room by nine, and the bar staff can turn cool if they feel shorted on tips, so tip on the card.
perfect: you want a cheap happy hour on St Marks.
insider: The back room takes private parties with food platters, and the General's cucumber cocktail is the one to order.

name: The Banc Bar Cafe (Murray Hill)
pitch: A stylish lounge in a 1920s bank building on 3rd Ave in Murray Hill, with sidewalk seating, live bands on weekends and a happy hour that starts at noon midweek. The cocktails and burger outshine the pasta, so lean on drinks, the coconut shrimp and the profiteroles.
perfect: you want live music and cocktails in Murray Hill.
insider: Sundays bring twenty-three dollar bottles of wine, and happy hour begins at noon Wednesday through Friday.

name: The Blind Barber
pitch: A barbershop on 10th St with a cocktail bar hidden behind it, chill before 10 PM and loud once the DJ starts on Thursday through Saturday nights. The cocktails are fair for Manhattan, the air conditioning is serious, and the door can be strict and unfriendly late.
perfect: you want a speakeasy with a haircut attached.
insider: Come between eight and ten for a quiet drink, and book Maria if you actually want the haircut.

name: The Bowery Electric
pitch: A bi-level rock club on the Bowery with a downstairs room whose acoustics make any show sound good, plus dance parties that start late. Beers are moderately priced, there is Guinness on tap, and there is no food, so eat first.
perfect: you want a small loud show downstairs.
insider: The downstairs room has the better sound, and the dance parties do not get going until around 11 PM.

name: The Cabin NYC
pitch: A rustic cabin of a restaurant on 4th St that redecorates for every season, with a menu printed on vinyl records and an indoor swing. Come for happy hour and shareable plates like the maple-glazed bacon steak rather than a serious dinner, and bring a date.
perfect: you want a cozy, kitschy date-night drink.
insider: Order the glazed bacon steak to share, and ask about the seasonal cocktails before they rotate out.

name: The Cabinet
pitch: A dark, intimate mezcal bar on 9th St near Avenue C, its shelves lined cabinet-style with bottles and staffed by bartenders who will teach you the difference between them. The smoky margarita and Oaxacan old fashioned are the anchors, with guacamole and crispy tacos to keep you going.
perfect: you want to learn mezcal from someone who cares.
insider: Order the Chixa Tapacho, and note the bar turns into a Christmas pop-up for the holiday season.

name: The Cøøper Sill
pitch: A whiskey bar on 2nd Ave with the bottles arranged by region, barrel-aged cocktails and better-than-pub food, including tots and a well-seasoned burger. The happy hour runs until 8 PM with three-dollar sliders and sidewalk seating, which is the cheapest good afternoon in the neighborhood.
perfect: you want whiskey, sliders and a sidewalk seat before eight.
insider: Happy hour until 8 PM gets you a six-dollar beer and three-dollar chicken or pork sliders.

name: The Grafton
pitch: An Irish pub that takes its sport seriously, with a proper pint of Guinness, a patio out back and bartenders who stay friendly when the room is packed. Drinks are not cheap and the patio shuts around 10, so claim a table inside before a big match.
perfect: the rugby is on and you want a real pint.
insider: Doors open at 9 on weekend mornings for early kickoffs, and a solo seat at the bar is the easiest way in.

name: The Gray Mare
pitch: A dark, wood-lined tavern on 2nd Ave where the lighting and the drinks do the heavy lifting and conversation still works at the bar. The kitchen is fine rather than memorable, so come for the long weekday happy hour and treat the food as a side quest.
perfect: you want a dim bar where you can actually talk.
insider: Happy hour runs weekdays from 3 to 8, and the calamari is big enough to split.

name: The Hairy Lemon Sports Bar
pitch: The Ave B sports pub that stays on its feet when a Knicks game fills every inch, with wings and shepherd's pie that hold up and bartenders who keep pouring. Bathrooms get rough late and you may get nudged to order quickly, but the energy on a big game night is hard to beat.
perfect: the game matters and you want a loud room.
insider: There is a side room you can book for a birthday, and the wings are the order.

name: The Immigrant
pitch: A candlelit sliver of an old tenement on 9th St with an eclectic wine list, generous pours and a charcuterie board built for two. Service runs hot and cold lately, with some nights warm and others brisk about turning tables, so go early on a weeknight and settle in at the bar.
perfect: a second-date glass of wine by candlelight.
insider: There are no reservations and the cocktail list is short, but the espresso martini is the one to order.

name: The Izakaya
pitch: A narrow 6th St izakaya that fries with a light hand, from silky agedashi tofu to chicken nanban, and the set menus for two or four take the ordering out of your hands. It leans rich and fried, and the bill climbs fast, so bring an appetite and someone to split it with.
perfect: you want sake and small plates without decisions.
insider: Order the addictive cabbage twice, and note it stays open until 2 on Thursdays.

name: The laurels
pitch: A 2nd Ave bar and brunch spot where the servers carry the place, the sidewalk tables fill on summer nights, and drinks run cheap until 7 even on Fridays. The eggs are a gamble, so lean toward the crispy chicken sandwich, the French toast and the truffle fries.
perfect: a sunny sidewalk table and a cheap early cocktail.
insider: The booths are tiny, so ask for a regular table or sit outside.

name: The Library
pitch: A graffiti-covered dive on Ave A with B movies on the back wall, books on the shelves and a jukebox that leans alt. Beers are cheap and strong drinks are stronger, but the bartenders run the room their way, so arrive with the right attitude and tip up front.
perfect: you want a cheap drink and a movie on the wall.
insider: Grab a table in the back where the movies play, and skip the jukebox on a staff birthday night.

name: The Mayfly
pitch: A roomy Houston St bar that does bottomless brunch, dollar wings, trivia and a lot of private parties, with mac and cheese and a solid burger to soak it up. When a party takes over the back the noise and the wait climb, so for a quiet lunch check the room first and stick to beer.
perfect: you need a bar that will host your whole group.
insider: Party bookings get to run their own playlist, and there are no spending minimums.

name: The Penny Farthing
pitch: An exposed-brick 3rd Ave tavern that splits into a bar side and a dining side, with brunch that overdelivers and daily drink specials worth planning around. The door and the host can be inconsistent about who waits and who must order food for a table, so a reservation on busy nights saves friction.
perfect: a cheap espresso martini on a Wednesday.
insider: Five-dollar espresso martinis on Wednesdays and Aperol spritzes on Thursdays, both after 4.

name: The Smith
pitch: The big, busy 3rd Ave standby that gets the crowd-pleasers right, from the double burger and truffle mac to a warm pretzel with beer cheese that stalls the whole table. It fills up and the tables get tight, so book ahead and leave room for the sticky toffee pudding.
perfect: a group dinner nobody will argue about.
insider: The ricotta gnocchi runs small, so order two if it is your main, and there is a photo booth downstairs.

name: The Spotted Owl Tavern
pitch: A vintage-feeling Ave A bar with a pool table in the back that always has a game going and chess, backgammon and Yahtzee behind the counter if you ask. Bartenders can be curt on a bad night, so come early in the week when the room is calm and the table is open.
perfect: a game of pool on a quiet Tuesday.
insider: Ask the bartender for a board game, and expect the pool table to be contested Thursday through Saturday.

name: The Stone
pitch: John Zorn's music-only room for experimental and avant-garde sets, where a different musician curates each month and every dollar at the door goes to the players. Expect folding chairs in tight rows, no food or drink and sets that start on time and finish by 10.
perfect: you want to hear something you cannot name yet.
insider: Tickets are $20, paid only at the door, and the shows wrap by 10 so you can go out afterward.

name: The Summit Bar
pitch: A warm, chandelier-lit cocktail bar on Ave C that doubles as a daytime cafe, with oysters at happy hour, a hummus platter people fixate on and a house dog who may join your table. The regulars are treated like family, and the staff mostly extend that to newcomers too.
perfect: a quiet cocktail far enough east to feel secret.
insider: Doors open at 9 in the morning Tuesday through Saturday, and the popcorn is a trap you will not regret.

name: The Ten Bells
pitch: A dark Broome St den for natural wine and Spanish-leaning tapas, with a dollar-oyster happy hour that runs on weekends too. Seating is first come, first served and nobody will explain that, so grab any open seat, check your bill, and order the steak tartare.
perfect: a cheap oyster and a funky glass before dinner.
insider: Happy hour runs on weekends too, and the mushroom croquetas and patatas bravas are the tapas to start with.

name: The Wayland
pitch: A rustic corner bar at the far end of 9th St where the Sazerac is dry and precise and the happy-hour oysters come small and briny. It is tight inside and the bar gets rowdy, so aim for the big bench by the window if you are more than two.
perfect: a serious cocktail without a serious room.
insider: The window bench by the piano is the only spot for a group, so reserve it for a 4:30 start.

name: The Winslow
pitch: A gin-focused British pub on 14th St with a long list of martinis and tonics, a stage for live bands and a back room that handles 30 people without a fuss. Early evenings can be oddly strict about table service when a band is due, so for a casual group drink sit at the bar.
perfect: you want a proper gin martini and a band later.
insider: Book the Back Room for a party and you get your own bartender for the night.

name: The Wren
pitch: A rustic Bowery barroom with sharp, fairly priced cocktails and hearty pub food that also does a strong weekend brunch of French toast and thick-cut bacon. Management keeps a tight hand on the room, so pace yourself if you want to stay for a second round.
perfect: a late drink on the Bowery that still feels warm.
insider: Walk-ins get squeezed in even near closing, but a reservation gets you a table rather than a standing spot at the bar.

name: The York
pitch: A small, friendly Ave B pub with a smashburger that outpunches its price and a happy-hour combo of burger, fries and a beer that is one of the best deals in the neighborhood. Order at the bar, grab whatever seat is free and do not skip the Caesar or the brussels sprouts.
perfect: you want a great cheap burger and a stiff drink.
insider: The happy-hour combo comes with Tecate or Coors, and the breakfast sandwich is quietly better than the burger.

name: Tile Bar
pitch: A tiny corner dive on 1st Ave with a jukebox, a cheap happy hour and a crowd that skews older and local. The bartenders set the terms, which lately means one tab for a big group and no patience for questions, so keep it small and quiet and you will be fine.
perfect: you want a cheap beer with no scene at all.
insider: Groups are made to run a single tab, so bring two friends, not eight.

name: Tre
pitch: A small Ludlow St Italian spot known for a Thursday night deal of three courses and two hours of unlimited wine at a price that includes the tip. The pastas swing from very good to gloopy depending on the night, so stick to the carbonara and the spicy sausage vodka pasta and book ahead.
perfect: a long, boozy dinner on a budget.
insider: Walk-ins can usually land two seats at the bar, and the bruschetta is the appetizer to split.

name: Tuome
pitch: Chef Chen's 5th St dining room does inventive Asian-leaning cooking, with snow crab noodles, scallop dumplings and a lamb that regulars still talk about. The prix fixe weeks draw mixed feelings and the courses lean fried, so order from the regular menu and start with the Tom Yum tomatoes.
perfect: a celebration dinner that still feels downtown.
insider: Closed Sunday and Monday, and the beignets are the dessert people remember.

name: Two Perrys
pitch: A warm little Ave C bar run by its owners, where the cocktails are built with care and the burger has a quiet reputation as one of the city's best. It is only open Wednesday through Saturday, and the hospitality is the kind that makes you plan your week around it.
perfect: you want the owners to pour your drink.
insider: Only open Wednesday through Saturday from 5, so check the day before you walk over.

name: Upstate
pitch: A tiny 1st Ave oyster bar where the fish comes in daily with no freezer in sight and the oysters are the reason to go. Six oysters and a draft for $13 from 5 to 7 fills the room by half past, so book or arrive right at opening.
perfect: oysters and a beer before a real dinner.
insider: Happy hour is chef's choice, three East Coast and three West Coast, and a little slice of cake arrives with the check.

name: Verlaines
pitch: A Rivington St lounge that has run on lychee martinis for two decades, still cheap at happy hour and still packed by 8 on a Wednesday. The room is leafy and dim and takes groups of any size, but the deal is strong enough to sneak up on you.
perfect: a cheap, sweet martini to start a night out.
insider: Happy hour runs 5 to 10 and the bar fills around 7, so come early if you are more than three.

name: Vin Sur Vingt Wine Bar
pitch: A small French wine bar on 2nd Ave where the staff speak French, know the list cold and steer you to a glass without any fuss. Warm light, good music and tartines of the day make it easy to stay for one more.
perfect: an unhurried glass of French wine on a weeknight.
insider: Ask for the tartine of the day, and in winter the mulled wine is the move.

name: Webster Hall
pitch: The 1886 ballroom on 11th St that is still the neighborhood's big concert room, with multiple levels, several bars and security that keeps crowd surfers in check. Lines run long and cold and the door is strict on ID, so bring a passport if your license is from abroad.
perfect: the band you love is playing a big room.
insider: If the line is long, the hotel across the street has a clean public bathroom downstairs.

name: Westville
pitch: The Ave A branch of the vegetable-forward neighborhood standby, where a market plate of four sides is a full meal and the specials board is worth reading. Service is friendly and the bill splits easily for a group, though the kitchen has slipped on fish once or twice lately.
perfect: you want vegetables that feel like a treat.
insider: Build a market plate with the yucca fries and the kale, and weekend brunch runs until 4.

name: Whiskey Town
pitch: A small 3rd St party bar with DJs, a disco ball, pop hits and a staff that goes all out when you book a birthday. It is more dance floor than whiskey library despite the name, so come to move, not to sip.
perfect: a birthday that needs a disco ball.
insider: Themed nights like the Harry Styles party are the draw, and a cold Monday late is when the regulars come out.

name: Whitmans
pitch: A small 9th St burger counter known for the Juicy Lucy, a patty stuffed with pimiento cheese, plus a crisp smash burger and hand-cut fries. The fried pickles are strange at first and then impossible to stop eating, and there are games downstairs while you wait.
perfect: a cheese-stuffed burger on a casual night.
insider: A lettuce wrap is available off menu, and the loaded tots beat the sweet potato fries.

name: Winebar
pitch: A speakeasy-feeling Japanese wine bar on 1st Ave where a DJ spins records and the natural-wine list rotates often. The kitchen does chicken karaage, a katsu sando and udon, and they have dropped beer entirely, so budget around $40 a head and come for the wine.
perfect: wine, vinyl and a katsu sando on a Tuesday.
insider: Open Tuesday through Saturday from 6 to 11, and the sofas are the seats to claim for a group.

name: Wonderland Bar
pitch: A whimsical 2nd Ave cocktail bar where you might be seated inside a birdcage of flowers and the drinks arrive with a bit of theater. The Asian-leaning bar snacks like chicken skewers and pork dumplings are better than they need to be, and the music stays at a level where you can still talk.
perfect: a date that wants a little theater with the drinks.
insider: Ask for the birdcage table, and the Paper Plane comes with a surprise to start.

name: Yellow Rose Tex Mex
pitch: San Antonians run this 3rd Ave Tex-Mex room, and the queso, skillet cornbread and homemade tortillas are what to come for. The tacos and mole divide people sharply and the acoustics are rough, so sit at the bar, keep it to snacks and margaritas, and enjoy the service.
perfect: queso and a margarita at the bar.
insider: They host Spurs watch parties, and the lemon-filled donut is the dessert to finish on.

name: Yubu
pitch: A bright 7th St counter for yubu, fried tofu pockets stuffed with sushi rice and toppings like torched salmon, spicy tuna or bulgogi, at three for $10. It is a light lunch rather than a feast, with three vegan options and a mango matcha latte that earns its price.
perfect: a quick, cheap lunch that is not a sandwich.
insider: There is no restroom for guests, and a set of eight for $25 is the best value if you are two.

name: Yuca Bar
pitch: A long-running Ave A corner spot with open windows, Pan-Latin small plates and a happy hour that makes the cocktails cheap. The ceviches are the strength and the guacamole is the weak spot, and on late Thursdays the room gets too packed to reach the bar.
perfect: a happy-hour cocktail by an open window on Ave A.
insider: Shots are not part of happy hour, so stick to the $9 cocktails and the ceviche.

name: Zerza Moroccan Kitchen
pitch: A Moroccan counter inside Essex Market doing tagines, couscous and stuffed pita sandwiches with generous portions and a hug of a welcome. The chicken tagine has gone bland lately, so lean toward the lamb, the beef pita or the chicken tfaya and finish with mint tea.
perfect: a big, cheap lunch while wandering Essex Market.
insider: The stewed beef pita and the eggplant spread are the counter's best, and it closes at 8 most nights, 6 on Sundays.
